preview: An interview experience for an FTE role at Goldman Sachs detailing the online assessment, technical rounds, puzzles, and HR interview, along with preparation tips.
content:
Sagar Dholakia, CE B.Tech, 2018-2022
ssdholakia_b18@ce.vjti.ac.in
GOLDMAN SACHS INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE (FTE 2021)
Round 0 (Online Assessment):
The online assessment was held on HackerRank and there were a total of five sections. It
lasted for 135 minutes.
Section 1: Basic Programming (30 mins)
The first section consisted of two programming questions of easy to moderate difficulty.
For the first question, we were given an array of length 2^N (misprinted as 2N). Each element
in the array represents the strength of a player, and each consecutive player competes with the
other. The player with more strength wins, and if the strengths are equal, the second player wins
and proceeds to the next round. Then the winners compete with each other, till there is only
one player left. We had to print the maximum level each player could reach.
For example, arr = {1, 2, 4, 3}.
After the first round matches conclude, elements 2 and 4 proceed to the next round.
After the second round, element 4 is the winner of the tournament.
As we can see, elements 1 and 3 reach a maximum level of 0, 2 reaches a maximum level of 1,
and 4 reaches 2. The expected output is {0, 1, 2, 0}.
The second question was a 01 Knapsack based question, where we were given an array of
strings, and each string had some value to it. The total weight of the knapsack was predefined
as 30. We had to maximise the value by choosing some strings from the array, and appending
them to an empty string. We had to add spaces in between adjacent strings that we chose
and had to account for the length of the extra spaces as well.
For example, N=4, arr={“priorityqueue”, “linkedlist”, “binarytree”, “adjacencymatrix”},
val={5, 6, 9, 10}
The answer here would be 19, as we select the last two strings from the array. The total length
which we have used out of the given weight of 30 would be 10+1+15 = 26.
I was able to fully solve the first question and partially solve the second question.
Section 2: Problem Solving (25 mins)
The second section consisted of multiple-choice questions based on aptitude and maths
(topics like trigonometry, probability were included). There were a total of 8 questions, and
each question had a +5/-2 scoring scheme (+5 for correct answer, -2 for wrong answer). So it’s
better to leave a question if you’re unsure about it rather than making a guess.
Section 3: Advanced Programming (45 mins)
This section had one advanced programming question.
Given a graph, we can apply the operation an arbitrary number of times (possibly 0) to
transform the given graph into a complete graph. An operation is defined as follows -
1.
Pick any vertex from the graph.
2.
Remove all pre existing edges from the vertex to other vertices.
3.
Add edges to all other vertices except the ones we removed in the previous step.
For example, if we have 3 nodes (1, 2 and 3) and have only 1 edge between nodes 1 and 2. We
choose node 1, so the existing edge is removed, and the remaining edges are added. Then we
finally select node 2, and the 2 remaining edges are added and we have a complete graph.
I was able to solve this question partially.
Section 4: Subjective (15 mins)
The fourth section consisted of two subjective questions which were based on your behaviour
and instances of motivation in your life.
The first question described a situation in which your classmate drops out of a project at a
critical time, and the deadline is near. How would you handle this situation?
The second question asked about a time where you were so motivated to do a project that you
went over and above to complete the project that you’re working on, and achieved better
results.
Both these questions are very frequently asked in the online assessment of Goldman Sachs,
for Internship as well as for FTE, so you can prepare for them beforehand.
Section 5: Computer Science (20 mins)
The last section again had multiple choice questions, but questions in this section were based
on topics including OOPs, Operating Systems, and Computer Networks. There were a total
of 7 questions which followed the same scoring pattern as before, i.e. +5/-2 for each question.
Round 1 (Technical Interview):
11 candidates were shortlisted for the interview process.
The interview was conducted on Zoom, and we were provided with a link to HackerRank
CodePair, which is a shared IDE and Whiteboard.
I was first asked to introduce myself. After the introduction, I was asked about LCA (Lowest
Common Ancestor) of a Binary Tree. I explained what it was, then we discussed my approach
to find the LCA of 2 nodes whose values were given to us. After explaining my approach, I was
asked to write a pseudo code for the same and had to dry run the code with the input my
interviewer provided. She was satisfied with my code and explanation.
She then asked me a second question. Given one way connections of flight, I had to find the
starting airport which connects (directly or indirectly) all other airports.
For example, B → C, A → B, C → D, then the answer here is A, as we can reach every airport if
we start from airport A in the following order A →B → C → D.
We only discussed an approach to the problem; due to time constraints, I wasn’t asked to code
my approach. I gave a solution to check the indegree of each airport, and there should exist
exactly 1 airport having an indegree of 0. This should be our starting airport. It was guaranteed
that there are no loops, no disconnected components, and only one possible starting airport.
I was then asked if I had any questions for my interviewer. This round lasted for around 45
minutes.
Round 2 (Technical Interview):
After the first round, 6 candidates qualified for further rounds.
My second interview started with a puzzle. Given three bags containing only red balls, only
white balls, and a mix of red and white balls, respectively, all of them are initially unlabelled. I
was asked to find the minimum number of balls to be taken out in order to correctly label each
of the three bags.
For the second question, I was asked to Sort a Linked List. I came up with a solution of O(N^2)
which was based on Selection Sort, but my interviewer was expecting the optimal solution
which is based on Merge Sort. I was then asked different sorting methods, and had to explain a
few of them.
Lastly, I was asked whether or not I had any questions for my interviewer. This round too lasted
for 45 minutes.
Round 3 (HR + Technical Round):
Only 3 candidates reached the final round of the interview process.
In this round, I was again asked to introduce myself. The interviewer asked me how the
previous rounds were and which type of questions were asked. Then he started asking me
questions about where I live, and how I commuted to college before the pandemic struck. After
about 10 minutes, he gave me a puzzle to solve.
Given a robot at position (0,0) and facing north, it is given a sequence of instructions.
There were 3 specific commands -
R → Rotate the direction of the robot 90° clockwise,
L → Rotate the direction of the robot 90° anti clockwise,
G → Move the robot by 1 unit in whichever direction it is currently pointing at.
Now, if the given sequence of commands is repeated infinitely many times, whether the robot
will move outside a given bound or not.
We discussed the solution on a Whiteboard, and I was not asked to code my approach. Finally,
my interviewer asked if I had any questions for him. This round lasted for 30 minutes.
Verdict:
2 of the 3 candidates were offered FTE roles; I was one of them.
Preparation:
- For questions based on Data Structures and Algorithms, GeeksForGeeks and
InterviewBit are more than enough.
- Prepare for topics like DBMS, OS and OOPs, don’t leave them for the last minute.
System Design questions can also be expected in interviews.
- Be thorough with what you have mentioned in your resume.
- Polish your oratory skills. Sometimes you may know the answer, but may not be able to
articulate it into words.
Tips:
- Whenever discussing an approach to a question with your interviewer, don’t jump to the
optimal solution straightaway (even if you do know the optimal solution). The
interviewers want to see your ability to think and come up with solutions.
- Think out loud. Your interviewers are there to help you, so speak whatever is in your
mind, don’t give much thought to whether what you’re thinking is right or wrong.
- Be confident in what you say, and keep a smile on your face while talking. Body
language and behaviour is just as important as technical skills.
- If you are unsure about something, be honest about it and let your interviewer know.
- Research about the company, what it does, any current news related to the company.
Also, go through company specific GeeksForGeeks archives for information on what
type of questions are asked in the interviews.
- Always ask relevant questions at the end of your interviews when given the opportunity.
It shows your interest in the company.
- Sab kismat hai bro. Sometimes you will be asked harder questions than your
batchmates, or maybe even after answering all the answers, you won’t be selected.
Don’t be discouraged or disheartened, there is always something better waiting for you.
Keep calm and all the best!
